name: Larkbourne Ford
unique_feature: a packhorse bridge over a bell that rings under the water when carts cross
story: The bridge was built over the Toll's fallen clapper; nobody could move it, so they paved around it. Carters say a crossing that rings twice means rain.
encounter: none by day; two bandits shake down late travellers after dark

name: Ansel's Hedge Shrine
unique_feature: a hawthorn grown through a stone chair, with a Hearthstone in its lap
story: Hearth-Mother Ansel sat here and told the first story about a neighbour. The hawthorn took the chair over the centuries; villagers still leave a pie on Naming Day.
encounter: none; a pilgrim NPC sometimes rests here

name: The Tumbled Watch
unique_feature: a Warden tower lying on its side down a dry valley, its stair now a corridor
story: It fell in the Quiet Villages years when its garrison stopped being talked about. Bandits use the lying stair as a hall; the Wardens want their old bell back from it.
encounter: skirmisher bandits in the stair-hall, a caster on the fallen parapet; approach from the hilltop to see them first

name: Gosling Pit
unique_feature: a chalk pit camp with a stolen mill wheel as a table
story: The Larkbourne Boys dug in below the Chalk Hound because nobody looks down when they can look up. The wheel came from Pennywort's Mill; the miller wants it back more than the thieves punished.
encounter: a pack of bandits with a brute leader; a rear path from the Hound's eye lets you drop in behind

name: The Singing Yew
unique_feature: a hollow yew with a small bell grown into its heartwood, humming in any wind
story: A Tamwick child hung a bell in a sapling; the tree ate it in three hundred years. Hedge-wights from the barrow will not pass it, which the orchard-keepers count on.
encounter: safe ground; a place to lure barrow-wights and watch them turn away

name: Whitecut Falls
unique_feature: the Larkbourne dropping off the chalk scarp in a single white sheet toward the Mere
story: The scarp is the edge the Toll cut when it fell. Down-wolves den in the spray caves behind the water.
encounter: a down-wolf pack in the cave behind the falls; wet stone slows dodges

name: Bell Meadow Stones
unique_feature: three leaning bronze-streaked stones where pieces of the Toll's crown landed
story: Each stone bears part of an Oroth word. The Sayers read them one way, the Wardens another, and the sheep sleep against them because they are warm.
encounter: none; a survey point that reveals the map around the Toll

name: Foxglove Dell
unique_feature: a dry valley entirely purple with foxgloves around a hedge-witch's turf hut
story: The hedge-witch Tansy Cresswell grows what Merrowby pretends not to buy. Something has been digging up her yew berries at night.
encounter: bristlebacks rooting in the dell at dawn; a charger fight in a narrow valley with soft banks

name: The Wellspring
unique_feature: a Hearthstone set in the lip of the spring where the Larkbourne rises clear out of the end of the black glass bed, and sheep grazing the first green below it
story: Pilgrims going south fill a flask here and carry it to the line to pour out. The first clean water north of the ash, and the first Hearthstone a Foundling reaches in the living country.
hook: A pilgrim's flask comes back up the glass bed full, and the woman who filled it is written on the Chapter Roll as gone on.

name: Ash Watch
unique_feature: a Warden watchtower with a beacon fire-bowl kept laid, to be lit the night anything walks up the Glassbed
story: The Wardens raised a line of towers along the grey border after the Ash Winter; Ash Watch is the one nearest the Choir, and its keeper is changed every nine days so nobody grows used to the view.
hook: The beacon was lit last night and nobody on the Ash Watch roll admits to lighting it.

name: Hound Watch
unique_feature: a Warden tower on the south end of Hound Down with a bell hung in its crown to ring the alarm down the Vale
story: From Hound Watch the keeper can see the Choir's colossi, the piers at the head of the Stair and the whole length of the Vale, which is why the Wardens built it here and why its keepers drink.
hook: The keeper has started ringing the alarm at the colossi. He says they moved.

name: The Brow Beacon
unique_feature: the easternmost beacon of the Wardens' line, its fire-bowl on the highest chalk above the Hush
story: When the Brow Beacon burns, Rookdown shuts its doors and Bramcombe brings the flocks in. It was lit four times in a hundred years, and twice this spring.
hook: Lit twice this spring by a keeper who swears the Hush came up the cliff like a tide and went back down.

name: Orm's Long Barrow
unique_feature: a long barrow opened by robbers, its capstones stacked beside it like a dropped deck
story: Older than Hollin Barrow, whose first cist Orm Hollin dug. The robbers took nothing and stacked the stones neatly, which is what frightens the shepherds.
encounter: hedge-wights stand up among the stones at dusk
hook: The robbers left a roll in the cist older than the Wardens' own, and Tamwick is on it twice.

name: Hurdle Fold
unique_feature: a shepherds' summer camp inside a ring of woven hurdles, with a lambing lantern kept lit all night on a crook
story: Bram Down's shepherds live out here from lambing to shearing. The lantern on the crook is so the ewes know where the fold is in the dark.
encounter: down-wolves try the hurdles after dark
hook: The wolves have learned the lantern; the shepherds want somebody to sit the night with them and the crook.

name: Lamb's Bottom
unique_feature: a shepherd's stone hut in a dry valley that the down-wolves have taken for their den
story: The shepherd who built it walked south in the Quiet Villages years; the wolves moved in the winter after, and the Vale has let them keep it.
encounter: a down-wolf pack in the hut
hook: A bounty on the Lamb's Bottom pack, and in the hut a crook carved with a name the Roll struck.

name: The Last Field
unique_feature: a farmhouse left standing in a ploughed field that runs to the cliff edge, where the furrows go grey halfway down
story: The Southcotes ploughed this field to the Brow for three hundred years. The year the grey reached the middle furrow they left the plough in it and walked to Rookdown.
encounter: hedge-wights work the grey furrows at night
hook: The plough has moved a furrow since the Southcotes left it.

name: The Grey End
unique_feature: the southern end of the Briar, where the thorn runs down to the cliff and has gone grey to the root around a broken wardstone
story: Where the Thornmarch meets the Hush the thorn is dead and grey and does not fall down. Woodfolk come here to cut grey thorn for arrows that do not miss.
encounter: ash-wights wander up out of the Hush along the cliff after dark
hook: Both Briar pamphleteers want a grey thorn from the Grey End as evidence, for opposite reasons.

name: The Southgate Stone
unique_feature: a Hearthstone facing the Briar's south gate, where the Vale's carts went east when the gates still opened
story: One of the four Hearthstones the Briar's gates face. The wardstone over the gate reads HESK-THAEL VAEL; the Vale reads it as keep off and ties ribbons to it anyway.
hook: Someone has been leaving the south gate unbarred at night, from the inside.

name: Hanging Coombe
unique_feature: a bandit camp in a hollow of Rook Wood with stolen boundary-bells hung in the trees as a warning
story: The Larkbourne Boys' eastern gang steal the little bells the Vale hangs on boundary hawthorns, which is worse than it sounds: a boundary without its bell is a boundary nobody is keeping.
encounter: four bandits and the brute who leads them
hook: Take the boundary-bells back to their hedges; one of the hedges no longer bounds anything.

name: Hushwatch
unique_feature: three stones on the lip of the Brow set to frame the Hush, where the Vale comes to look at the grey and go home grateful
story: Vale families walk up on a clear evening to stand between the stones and look south. The custom is to say one name out loud before turning back.
hook: A child said a name between the stones that nobody in the Vale knows, and the name is on the Wardens' deep lines.

name: The Naming Stone
unique_feature: a Hearthstone where the downs' children are named on Naming Day, its face worn smooth by small hands
story: Every child born on the Brow is carried here in spring and named out loud to the stone, the shepherds and the sky. The stone keeps the names; the shepherds keep the party.
hook: The stone has a name worn into it that no child on the Brow was ever given.

name: The Flint Pits
unique_feature: a flint-diggers' camp among white spoil heaps, where the Vale's builders buy their flint by the cartload
story: The knappers dig shafts into the chalk and come up white to the eyebrows. They sell the Vale its walls and its sparks, and say the deepest shaft goes down into something that rings.
hook: The deepest shaft rings when struck; the knappers want a Sayer, a Warden or anyone braver than them to go down.

name: The Weighing Stone
unique_feature: a slab on three stones carrying a carters' weighing-beam, where the ridge road leaves the downs for the Wold
story: Dorrie Cooper weighs her hand-cart here going up and again at the top. The beam was set by the Tamwicks, who do not trust Woodfolk scales; the Woodfolk weigh again at the top.
hook: Dorrie's slate says the ridge road has eaten a cart and a half of goods in twenty years; the beam says it has not.

name: Wolf Holt
unique_feature: a sheepfold of flint walls on the downs' marsh edge that the down-wolves have taken back
story: Fallowfold's shepherds built it when the West Downs ran further west. The marsh came up and the wolves came with it.
encounter: a down-wolf pack in the fold
hook: The pack's leader wears a Warden's collar-bell, and the Wardens would like to know whose.

name: The Cress Bridge
unique_feature: a bridge of three chalk-white slabs on flint piers over the Cressbourne, with a coin wedged in every joint for luck
story: Carts to Tamwick cross here. The coins are Tamwick's toll to the water, paid in the Vale's way: nobody collects them, and nobody would dream of taking one.
hook: Somebody is taking the coins, one a night, and the Cressbourne has started to run low.

name: The Warden Barrow
unique_feature: the barrow of the first Wardens, its entrance kerb set with nine hand-bells that the youngest at the Rest rings on Tollday
story: The first Wardens were buried together on their own down so they could keep the Roll room in sight. Their bells are rung each Tollday by whoever is youngest at the Rest.
hook: The youngest at the Rest has stopped ringing the bells, because one of them rings back.

name: The Rod Stacks
unique_feature: a hazel-cutters' camp at the wood's edge with the season's rods stacked in wigwams to dry
story: Hazelcombe's cutters meet the Woodfolk here at the edge of the Wold to buy the rods. Neither side crosses the line of the stacks.
hook: The Woodfolk have stopped selling the Vale its rods, and the cutters want to know who in the Wold is saying no, and why.

name: The Roll Stone
unique_feature: a single standing stone at the foot of Wardens' Down with the four quiet villages cut into it and struck through
story: The Wardens read the Roll aloud here on Candle Night, name by name, and strike nothing: the four names were struck through by the hands that cut them.
hook: A fifth name has been cut beneath the four in a Warden's hand, and struck through, and nobody at the Rest will say whose.

name: The Old Sheepwash
unique_feature: a drystone wash-pool dammed across a dry spring-head, the sheep-gate still hung
story: Fallowfold's flocks were washed here before shearing for three hundred years. The spring went up the hill in the year Wynstead's meadows drowned, and the shepherds have carried buckets after it since.
hook: The spring is moving again, a yard a day, toward Fallowfold's gate.

name: The Pinfold
unique_feature: a round drystone pound for strayed beasts beside the Eastway, with a hand-bell hung on its gate
story: Merrowby's hayward pens the Vale's strays here until their owners pay a penny, ring the bell and take them home.
hook: Every morning there is one more sheep in the Pinfold than anybody put there, and nobody in the Vale will own it.

name: The Dewpond Fold
unique_feature: a shepherds' summer fold round a dew pond that nobody has ever seen empty or filling
story: Barrow Down's flocks are folded here from Naming Day to the Long Table and drink from the one water on the down that nobody dug.
hook: On still nights the dew pond shows the stars at noon, and the shepherds have stopped mentioning it.

name: The Hare Stone
unique_feature: a boundary stone with a hare cut on its Vale face and an oak leaf on its Wold face, both worn smooth by hands
story: Where the downs end and the Wold begins. Vale folk touch the hare going in and Woodfolk touch the leaf coming out; nobody has ever been seen to touch both.
hook: Somebody has cut a third mark on the top of the stone overnight, a bell, and left the chisel in the grass.

name: Tallow Barrow
unique_feature: a long barrow opened by treasure-diggers and walled up again from the inside
story: Diggers from Tollmere opened it in 1012 for grave-gold the Vale swears was never there. They came out without their spades and would not go back, and in the morning the entrance was walled.
encounter: hedge-wights come out of the barrow at night
hook: The new wall has a door-shaped gap in it this spring, and the chalk round the gap is warm.

name: The Warrener's Camp
unique_feature: a warrener's turf hut and ferret-hutches dug into the gorse under the Thornmarch
story: Rookdown's warrener keeps the downs' rabbits in check and sells their skins in Tamwick. He has not been seen at home since the Long Table.
encounter: none; the warrener's things and nobody home
hook: The ferrets will not go down one burrow, and every rabbit on the down comes out of it.

name: The Cliff Hearth
unique_feature: a Hearthstone on the Brow's last rise, with a fire kept for whoever comes up from the Hush
story: The Vale says the fire was lit for the drowned; the Wardens say it was lit for the Foundlings, before the Foundlings stopped coming. Rookdown keeps it because it has always been kept.
hook: The ash was warm on the morning the Foundling came up the Stair, and nobody on the Brow had lit it.

name: The Hush Steps
unique_feature: Oroth steps cut down the face of the Brow's cliff and stopping in the air above the water
story: Nobody knows what the Builders went down to. Rookdown's children dare each other to the last step, and the last step is always one further down than the last child reached.
hook: A lit lantern has been left on the last step, tied with a Sedgish lantern-knot.

name: The Cliff Graves
unique_feature: a row of graves along the cliff's edge, every headstone turned to face the Hush
story: Rookdown buries its drowned here, facing the water that took them, so they will see it coming if it comes back for the rest.
hook: One headstone has turned in the night to face inland.

name: Rook Mill
unique_feature: a sail-less windmill on the Brow's back whose millstone is heard grinding on still nights
story: Rookdown's mill lost its sails in the gale of 1030 and was never rigged again. The miller moved down to the village; the millstone stayed.
hook: Flour has been found on the mill floor, fine and grey, and it tastes of ash.

name: Candle Cross
unique_feature: a wayside Hearthstone where the Brow road crosses the drove, with a candle niche cut in each of its four faces
story: On Candle Night every farm on the Brow sends one candle here, and the crossroads is the brightest place on the downs until dawn.
hook: A candle has been burning in the north niche since midsummer, and it has not got any shorter.

name: The Last Look
unique_feature: a leaning stone and a pilgrims' bench on the last of the downs, looking out over the ash to the Choir
story: Pilgrims leaving the Vale stop here for their last look at green ground. Pilgrims coming back touch the stone and do not look round.
hook: The stone leans a little further toward the Choir every year; this year it moved a hand's breadth in one night.

name: Pennywort Bridge
unique_feature: a humpback bridge over the Larkbourne with a cracked millstone set in its parapet
story: The mill's first stone cracked on its first turn and was built into the bridge, so the Larkbourne would carry the bad luck down to the Mere.
hook: The cracked millstone has turned a quarter in the parapet, and there is fresh mortar dust in the road.

name: The Lambing Fold
unique_feature: a lambing shelter of hurdles on Bram Down, built new each spring on the same ground
story: Rookdown's ewes lamb here out of the wind off the Hush. The shepherds sleep in the fold for the fortnight and swear the down is warmer there than anywhere.
hook: A lamb was born in the fold this spring with a face as grey as ash, and the ewe that bore it belongs to nobody.

name: The Chalk Cell
unique_feature: a hermit's cell cut into the chalk of the Whitecut, with one window looking out over the Mere
story: A hermit lived here for forty years looking at the Spire across the water. The Vale brought her bread, and nobody asked her name.
hook: Bread left at the cell's door is being taken again, after thirty years.

name: The Turned Hut
unique_feature: a shepherd's hut half-buried in drifted ash on the Brow's west slope, its door facing away from the Choir
story: The Brow's shepherds will not graze within sight of the Choir. The last one who did left this hut, and the ash has had it since.
hook: There is fresh straw in the hut, and the ash round the door has been swept.

name: The Chalk Pit
unique_feature: a white pit dug into Bram Down's flank where Rookdown gets its chalk, the diggers' hut at its lip
story: Rookdown cobs its walls with chalk from here and marls its fields with the rest. The pit has been dug so long that the down has a bite out of it you can see from the Hush.
hook: A pick was found standing in the chalk face this spring with a Tallyman's mark on the haft.

name: The Hayward's Perch
unique_feature: a hayward's lookout on four stilts over the common fields south of Wynstead, a tally of strays cut into every post
story: Merrowby's hayward climbs it at first light to count what has got out of the folds, and cuts the count into the posts. The oldest cuts are at the top, where no hayward alive can reach.
hook: The newest cut on the south post is a notch under and a notch over, and the hayward says he did not cut it.

name: Hurdlegate Farm
unique_feature: a lived-in farmstead of whitewashed cob and thatch where the downs road leaves Ashwell, its yard gate made of old sheep-hurdles
story: The Hurdlegates have farmed the foot of the downs since before the Toll fell and keep the drove gate for Ashwell, which means opening it for every flock that comes down and being thanked by none of them.
hook: Somebody has been sleeping in the hay-loft and leaving the eggs they did not eat in a neat row on the sill.

name: Brow End
unique_feature: the last farmstead on the Brow before Rookdown, a long low house of flint with its back to the Hush wind and its byre door painted red
story: Brow End keeps the Brow's cattle through the winter in a byre with a red door, because the Brow's grandmothers said red keeps the grey off a beast, and nobody has lost a cow to the grey since, which proves nothing and settles everything.
hook: The byre door has been painted again overnight, red over red, and the pot is not the farm's.

name: Hatchmoor
unique_feature: a farmstead of chalk-block walls round a square yard on the open downs between the Hare and Hurdle and Bramcombe, its dovecote taller than the house
story: The Hatchmoors breed doves for the Wardens' line, one pair to each beacon, and can tell you which bird flew from which beacon by the ring on its leg and the look in its eye.
hook: A dove came home to the cote this week wearing the ring of a beacon that has not been manned in forty years.

name: Coldharbour
unique_feature: a farmstead in a fold of the downs below Hollin Barrow, its well-house roofed with turf and its walls ringed with the barrow's own fallen stones
story: Coldharbour was built with stones carried off the barrow, before anybody knew better, and every Tollday the farm puts one back on the mound, and the barrow keeps its own count of how many are still owed.
hook: The stone put back last Tollday was back in the farm wall by morning.

name: Pennywort Fields
unique_feature: a miller's farm on the road out of Merrowby to Pennywort's Mill, a thatched house among wheat strips with a quern set by the door for anybody to use
story: The mill's own fields, farmed by the miller's cousins, who grind what they need on the door-quern rather than pay the mill, which is a family argument four generations old.
hook: The door-quern has been turning at night, and in the morning there is cold flour in the trough and no grain gone from the store.

name: Ashway Farm
unique_feature: the southernmost farm in the Vale, on the road from Pilgrim's Ash to Bramcombe, its fields running up to the edge of the grey and ploughed right to it
story: Ashway ploughs to the grey's edge every spring and the grey is a furrow further off by harvest, every year, which the farm takes as its due and the Order takes as a question.
hook: This spring the last furrow was ploughed, and the grey was on the near side of it in the morning.

name: The Last Farm
unique_feature: a farmstead at the Grey End where the downs stop at the Hush, lived in by one old woman who keeps a lamp in the window facing the grey all night
story: Every other house at the Grey End is empty. Maud Rookwell stays because somebody should be the last farm, and keeps the lamp lit so that whatever walks out of the grey at night sees a window before it sees a village.
hook: The lamp was found out one morning and the window open, and Maud says she did not open it.

name: Southgate Farm
unique_feature: a farmstead by the Southgate Stone on the drove to the Brow, with a stone trough in the yard where every drover waters his beasts and pays in gossip
story: Southgate takes no coin for its water, only news, and the farmer's wife has the most complete account of the Vale's comings and goings anybody keeps, written in a hand only her daughters can read.
hook: A drover watered his beasts at the trough last week and paid with news of a village nobody has heard of.

name: Ridgeway Farm
unique_feature: a farmstead on the ridge road where the Vale's fields give out against the Wold's first oaks, half its fences Vale hurdles and half Woodfolk wattle
story: Ridgeway is Vale on the side that faces Tamwick and Woodfolk on the side that faces the Hollow, and the family keeps both customs so thoroughly that it keeps two Long Tables and two naming-days a year.
hook: The oak at the Wold end of the yard has started putting out Vale apple blossom.

name: Fallowgate
unique_feature: a farmstead on the road between Wynstead and Fallowfold whose fields have lain fallow for three years by a vow nobody in the family will explain
story: The Fallowgates made a vow the year the Ninth Waystone's counts stopped, and have not sown since, and live on what the orchard and the bees give them, and are the best-fed family in the Vale.
hook: The fallow field has come up in wheat on its own this spring, in straight drills, as if sown.

name: Larkfield
unique_feature: a farmstead between Wynstead and Merrowby with a lark's nest left undisturbed in the middle of its best field, fenced off with a ring of hurdles
story: The Larkfields found a lark nesting in the wheat the spring the Toll fell, and left it, and a lark has nested in the same spot every spring since, and the ring of hurdles round it has never once been ploughed.
hook: There are two nests in the ring this spring, and the second one is empty and warm.

name: Hazel Bottom
unique_feature: a farmstead in a hazel-hedged bottom under Hollin Barrow on the road to Hazelcombe, with nut-baskets drying on every sill
story: Hazel Bottom sells cob-nuts in Tamwick and hazel rods to the Wold, and its hedges are the oldest in the Vale, laid and re-laid for three hundred years by the same family's hands.
hook: A stretch of hedge has been laid overnight, beautifully, in a style the family's grandmother said died with her grandmother.

name: Cress Mill
unique_feature: an undershot mill wheel in a stone leat off the Cressbourne below Cressbourne, grinding the Vale's barley for the Tamwick brewers
story: The Cress Mill grinds barley for the brewers and nothing else, by an old agreement with the Tallymen that nobody has read in a century, and the miller will not grind a sack of wheat for his own bread.
hook: The wheel has been turning backward at night, against the water, and the barley in the hopper comes out as whole grain.

name: Lark Mill
unique_feature: a timber mill on the Larkbourne below Wynstead, its wheel turning in a leat lined with the Larkbourne's own grey stones
story: Lark Mill grinds for Wynstead and Merrowby both, and its miller keeps the only clock between them, a water-clock off the leat, by which both villages have agreed to be late.
hook: The mill's water-clock has started keeping a different hour from the Toll's, a quarter behind, and the Larkbourne has risen to match it.

name: The Cider Shrine
unique_feature: a Vale hedge-shrine in the last field before the oaks, where Tamwick folk going into the Wold leave a cup of cider on the stone
story: The Wold gives no leave and asks none, which makes Vale folk uneasy, so Tamwick thanks it in advance instead: a cup of cider on the stone at the edge of the last field, left full, and found empty coming home.
hook: The cup has been left full a fortnight, and the Tamwick carters say the Wold has stopped drinking with them.

name: The Last Dry Mile
unique_feature: a milestone on the Westway where the downs' chalk gives out and the reedfolk's boardwalk begins, cut with the miles to Merrowby on one face and a lantern on the other
story: Vale carters and reedfolk meet at the stone and swap loads, because no Vale carter will take a wheel onto the boardwalk and no reedfolk will pull a cart. The lantern face is the reedfolk's: past it, carry a light.
hook: The lantern cut on the stone's face has been blacked in with soot overnight, which is the reedfolk's sign for a drowned person's lantern.

name: The Long Table Bench
unique_feature: a bench of chalk blocks on a flagged plinth on the downs road, a cairn of flints beside it, looking north down the Vale to the Mere
story: Walkers going up to the Hare and Hurdle sit here for the view of the whole Vale laid out to the water. Each Long Table the inn's people carry a flint up from the feast and add it to the cairn, one for every harvest the downs have kept.
encounter: a bristleback roots along the downs road at dawn
hook: Somebody has been leaving a place laid on the bench, a plate, a cup and a slice of pie, as if for a guest at the Long Table who has not come.

name: Ribbon Meg's Fire
unique_feature: a pedlar's camp on the Brow road, a painted cart and a fire, ribbons for sale hung on a line between two stakes
story: Ribbon Meg has worked the Brow's farms for thirty years with ribbon, thread, pins and gossip, and camps at this bend because it is a day's walk from Bramcombe and a day's walk from Rookdown, and she does not like either of them enough to sleep there.
hook: Meg has sold nothing but candles this month, one to every farm on the Brow, and every farm has set its candle in the window that faces south.

name: The Hound's Bowl
unique_feature: a hedge-shrine below the Chalk Hound where the Vale leaves a bowl of water for the hill figure on hot days
story: The Chalk Hound is scoured every seven years by everyone who can hold a rake, and in the years between the Vale leaves him water when the weather is hot, because a dog cut into a hill is still a dog and should not be thirsty.
hook: The bowl has been drunk dry every morning of this hot spell, and there are chalk paw-prints on the stone, each the size of a cartwheel.

name: The Millers' Stone
unique_feature: a broken milestone on the mill road, its top lying face-up at its foot with 'Pennywort's Mill, 1 mile' still on it
story: The cart carrying the mill's first stone up from the quarry broke this milestone when the millstone slid off it, which was the first bad luck, and the stone cracked on its first turn, which was the second. The milestone was left broken, to keep count.
hook: The broken top has been set back on its stump overnight, and the mile cut on it now reads nothing at all.

name: Gorse Hut
unique_feature: a shepherd's summer hut of flint and turf under the gorse on the Brow, with a drystone fold for the ewes beside it
story: Rookdown's shepherds summer their ewes on this corner of the Brow and sleep in the hut in turns. It is the last roof before the Thornmarch's gorse, and the warrener from the camp below used to come up for his supper.
encounter: down-wolves circle the fold after dark
hook: The warrener who went missing at the Long Table has been sleeping in the hut, the shepherd says, and will not come out, and asks only for rabbit.

name: The Boys' Lookout
unique_feature: a bandits' lookout fire at the edge of Rook Wood where the Larkbourne Boys' eastern gang watch the Brow road, a stolen boundary-bell hung over it
story: The Larkbourne Boys' eastern gang keep a lookout here for the Hanging Coombe, a fire and a sentry, with a view of the Brow road from Bramcombe to Rookdown. Travellers who see the fire go round by the fields.
encounter: two bandits keep the lookout after dark
hook: The lookouts have started ringing their stolen boundary-bell whenever anybody comes up the road, and they say it is a warning to the travellers, not to the gang.

name: The Wardens' Halt
unique_feature: a Warden patrol's halting-place on the Bramcombe road below Hound Watch, a fire and a lean-to and the pole where the patrol hangs its hand-bell while it rests
story: The Wardens' patrols out of Hound Watch rest here on their way down the Vale. Down-wolves come up out of Lamb's Bottom after dark, so the halt is never left without a fire, and the patrol's bell is hung on the pole to be rung if the fire has to be left.
encounter: down-wolves come up out of Lamb's Bottom after dark
hook: A patrol came down and found another patrol's fire already lit at the halt and its bell on the pole, and nobody from the Rest was out that night.

name: The Grey-Wind Cairn
unique_feature: a lone cairn on the down's shoulder above Fallowfold, a rag tied to a stick in its top for the shepherds to read the wind by
story: When the rag on the cairn streams north the wind is off the ash, and the West Downs' shepherds bring the flocks in to Fallowfold's pond to wash the grey out of the fleeces before it settles.
hook: The rag has streamed north all week, and there has been no wind at all.

name: The Garrison Shrine
unique_feature: a Warden shrine at the roadside for the Tumbled Watch's lost garrison, a stone with nine names cut on it where the patrols stop
story: The Tumbled Watch fell in the Quiet Villages years because its garrison stopped being talked about. The Wardens raised this shrine where the road can see the fallen tower, and every patrol that passes says the nine names aloud.
hook: Somebody has hung the Tumbled Watch's own bell back on the frame, the bell the bandits took from it, and the bandits in the watch swear they still have it.

name: The Turned-Back Fire
unique_feature: the fire where Warden patrols rest after turning back at the Last Hearth; it went out when the last patrol left, and the cups are still set round it
story: Patrols on the grey side turn back at the Last Hearth and stop here for the night, the first fire on the Vale side, before they walk home. The rule is to leave the cups set round it, so the next patrol knows how many came back. Dann's spear is still leaning by the cold hearth where he left it before he went south.
encounter: ash-wights stray over the grey border to the cold fire after dark
hook: One cup at the cold fire is full every morning, and warm.

name: The Gossip Stones
unique_feature: three stones by the Merrowby road where the Vale's women stop on market day to talk, each worn into a seat
story: Gossip is a kind of prayer, the Vale says, and this is where it is prayed. The three stones are the Vale's oldest seats, and whatever is said on them by noon is known in every kitchen from Wynstead to Tamwick by supper.
hook: Nobody has sat on the middle stone since spring, and anyone who does forgets what they were about to say.

name: The Malting Floor
unique_feature: the roofless malting house below the Hanger where the Vale's barley was sprouted for Tamwick's brewers, one gable standing over the flagged floor
story: Before Cress Mill took the brewers' barley, it was malted here, spread on the flags and turned by hand until it sprouted. The house fell in when the malting moved, and the flags have been grassing over ever since.
encounter: two Larkbourne Boys have taken the malting for a hideout
hook: The floor has sprouted again this spring, barley coming up between the flags in the shape of a man lying down.

name: Toll View
unique_feature: a bench on a flagged plinth on the Stride road where the Cracked Toll is first seen whole, a cairn of bronze-streaked stones beside it
story: Travellers coming off the Long Stride stop here for their first sight of the Toll, the bronze bell forty metres tall and half sunk in the hill. The cairn is made of stones with bronze in them from where the crown broke, and the Vale is very proud of it.
hook: The bench hums when you sit on it now, since the Toll began to hum, and the old men of Stride's Foot who sit there have started humming back.

name: The Dole-House
unique_feature: the roofless dole-house below Hollin Barrow where the Barrow Reeve's alms were given out, one gable standing and a stone coffin inside it for the bread
story: The Barrow Reeve kept the barrow and gave alms at its foot, bread in a stone coffin that the poor lifted the lid of themselves, so nobody need be seen taking. The Reeve has been in the barrow a long time, and not resting, and the dole-house fell in.
encounter: a hedge-wight works the verge after dark
hook: Alms have been left in the stone coffin, bread and a penny, and in the morning the penny is gone and the bread is not.

name: The Quiet Mile
unique_feature: a waystone on the West Walk road cut with the names of the four quiet villages and a mile to each that nobody can walk
story: The Wardens set the stone so the names on the Roll are read by everyone who passes: Mullbourne, Harewell, Larkstead and Gosford, each with its mile cut beside it, though no road goes there any more and no map shows them.
hook: A fifth name has been cut below the four, fresh, and the Wardens have not struck any village from the Roll.

name: The Rubbing Stones
unique_feature: three leaning stones in a hollow by the Tamwick road, polished smooth at knee height by the flanks of bristlebacks
story: Bristlebacks come to the hollow at dawn to rub the burrs out of their hair on the stones, and have leaned them over doing it. Tamwick's carters pass the hollow at a trot before sunrise and a walk after.
encounter: bristlebacks come to the stones to rub at dawn
hook: The stones have been rubbed smooth at the height of a man's shoulder, higher than any bristleback stands.

name: The Drove Gate Toll
unique_feature: a bandits' fire at the drove gate on the downs road, a cart run across the way to close it, the Larkbourne Boys' stolen boundary-bells hung on the gatepost
story: The Hurdlegates keep the drove gate for Ashwell and open it for every flock. The Larkbourne Boys keep it now for themselves, on the days they are in funds, and shut it with a cart and ask a toll of anything with wheels.
encounter: two Larkbourne Boys and a bruiser keep the gate by day
hook: The Boys have started asking travellers where they are going and turning some of them back for their own good, and will not say what they have seen on the down.

name: The Lone Barrow
unique_feature: a roofless barrow-house in the Brow's last fields, its stone coffin lying open inside, a Warden's grave from the first years
story: One of the first Wardens asked not to be buried with the others on their down but out here on the Brow, where the ash would come first, so that someone who had kept the Roll would be facing it. His coffin was found open in the Quiet Villages years and nobody has closed it.
encounter: a hedge-wight works the barrow's field after dark
hook: The ploughmen say something works the barrow's field after dark, turning the soil with its hands.

name: The Mill-Down Fold
unique_feature: a hurdle fold on the down above Pennywort's Mill, its hurdles staked into the chalk, sheep in it at dusk
story: The Pennyworts fold their sheep on the down above the mill that turns with no water, and swear the flock settles better there than anywhere, because of the hum it makes coming up through the chalk.
hook: The sheep have been found every morning lying in a ring facing the mill, and not one of them will be driven down the hill.

name: Ansel's Dew-Well
unique_feature: a dew-well on the East Downs, a round of flints about a shallow stone basin with a cup on a chain, where the Vale says Hearth-Mother Ansel stopped to drink
story: Hearth-Mother Ansel, who first told a story about a neighbour, is said to have stopped at this well on the down and told the story to whoever was drinking. The water is only dew, gathered in the night on the flints, and there is always exactly one cup of it.
hook: There have been two cups of water in the basin every morning this spring, and the Vale cannot decide which of them is for whom.

name: The Barrow-Flock Fold
unique_feature: a hurdle fold on the Brow above Coldharbour with a turf shelter at its side, where the barrow's own flock is penned and never counted
story: Coldharbour keeps a small flock for the barrow, the stones owed to it being too slow to pay, and pens it here in sight of the mound. The flock is never counted, because counting it would be saying how much is owed.
hook: Somebody counted the flock last week, out loud, and in the morning there was one sheep fewer and one stone more on the barrow.

name: The Ploughman's Grave
unique_feature: a single Vale grave at the Brow's cliff end, a mound with a board at its head, the ploughman who ploughed the last field buried facing the Hush
story: The last field on the Brow was ploughed to the cliff's edge by a Rookdown man who said a field is ploughed to its end or not at all. He asked to be buried at the end of it, facing the Hush, so he could see if anything came up it.
hook: The board at the grave's head has been turned round in the night to face the Vale.

name: The Naming Well
unique_feature: a wellhead of chalk blocks on the Brow between Candle Cross and the Naming Stone, where the water for Naming Day is drawn
story: Every child named at the Naming Stone is washed first in water drawn here, from the one well on the Brow that has never gone dry. The bucket is kept on its hook and used for nothing else.
hook: The bucket has been found on the wellhead full every morning this month, and there has not been a child born on the Brow since the Long Table.

name: The Brow Lichen Ring
unique_feature: a small ring of three leaning stones on the open down above the Brow, yellow with lichen, a ring of mushrooms inside them
story: The Brow shepherds bring their ewes past the ring in spring and never through it. The stones are older than the Vale's names for anything, and the lichen on them is said to grow only where somebody has been promised something.
hook: The mushroom ring inside the stones has come up twice as wide this spring, and it now takes in one of the stones.

name: The Wynstead Ditch Camp
unique_feature: a roadside bandits' camp in a dry ditch on the Wynstead road, a smoky fire, two bedrolls and a stolen milestone used for a table
story: Two bandits worked the Wynstead road for a season from a ditch within sight of the Fallowfold, and took the milestone from the verge for their table because the Wardens used it to tell them how far they had to ride.
encounter: two roadside bandits camp in the ditch by day
hook: The milestone the bandits took has been carried back to the verge in the night, and the bandits have not moved the camp.

name: The Hound's Swallet
unique_feature: a swallow-hole in the south flank of Hound Down where a lost stream went into the chalk, its lip worn smooth by the pads of wolves
story: The Vale says the Chalk Hound was cut on the down to keep one hound asleep, and that the hound sleeps here, where the old bourne went under. The Hounders scour the figure white every seventh summer so that it stays asleep. This is the eighth summer. The down wolves have been coming up out of the swallet in fours since the Long Table, bolder than wolves are, and the scourer who went down after them at the last scouring has never come up.
encounter: down wolves lie up in the mouth by day and hunt out of it at night; below, the pack, the pelters who follow it, and the Old Hound in the deepest chamber
hook: A rake-head is wedged in the rock of the swallet's throat, tied with a scourer's white cord, and the cord runs down into the dark.

name: The Drovers' Pound
unique_feature: a six-sided pound of oak stakes on the open down, built by the eastern drovers to hold a flock overnight against the wolves, with a wolf pack denned inside it
story: When the Briar's gates still opened, the drovers took the Brow flocks east and penned them here the last night on Vale ground, behind a palisade the wolves could not jump. The gates shut and the drove stopped. The down wolves found the pound empty and warm and dry, and have kept it since, which the drovers call the only joke the down has ever made.
encounter: a pack of down wolves in the pound, more of them after dark
hook: The drovers' tally-board is still nailed inside the gate, the last flock counted in and never counted out.

name: The Lime Bay Kilns
unique_feature: a chalk cut above Lime Bay with two squat flint lime kilns built into its foot, their draw-arches smoking and the ground round them white as a bakehouse floor
story: Cressbourne's limeburners have burned the down to quicklime here since before the Toll fell: lime for the Vale's cob and whitewash, lime for its fields, and lime for the headlands on the grey's edge, which the south farms swear keeps the grey a furrow off. Hedda Limeburner keeps the kilns now with her son, and has not sent a cart south since spring.
encounter: the limeburners work the kilns by day; bristlebacks come down the cut at dusk after the burners' scraps
hook: The south cart stands loaded by the kilns with its shafts on the ground: a season's lime for Ashway, and nobody to take it.

name: The Brow Long Table
unique_feature: a hundred paces of trestle tables set end to end along the crest of Bram Down, and at the table's foot a mound of turf with the handles of buried bells standing up out of it
story: Every farm on the Brow sits down together here at harvest, one table from Rookdown to Bramcombe, and the Table-Warden sets a place for every household on the Wardens' Roll. A family whose line has ended has its bell buried at the table's foot, so the Brow can say it is still there. This spring one of the bells was dug up and taken.
encounter: the Table-Warden keeps the ground between Long Tables; crows at the table's foot
hook: One hole at the table's foot, where the Hurdwell bell was buried, and a Larkbourne boot-print in the turf beside it.

name: The Bram Down Wheelhouse
unique_feature: a shepherd's hut on four iron wheels, dragged up onto the high down for lambing, with a ring of hurdles about it and a tar-pot on the step
story: Bramcombe's head shepherd lives out on the down in a hut on wheels from lambing to shearing, and moves it with the flock. Old Enid Drove has had it forty summers and the wheels have never once turned downhill of the Naming Well, because she says a shepherd who can see the Hush from her step does not sleep.
encounter: the shepherd by day; down wolves come to the hurdles on the darkest nights
hook: Enid has been counting her ewes twice every evening, and the second count is always one ewe more.

name: The Southcote Lynchets
unique_feature: old field terraces stepped down the Brow's last slope toward the Hush, each lip hedged, the Southcotes' dead buried at the hedge line with their tools, and fresh furrows in the terraces every morning
story: Before the Southcotes ploughed the Last Field they farmed these terraces, and they buried their own at the hedge line as the Vale does, each with a spade or a scythe to be known by. The family walked to Rookdown when the grey came up the field. The dead did not go with them. Every morning the terraces are turned a little further toward the grey.
encounter: hedge-wights work the terraces from dusk to dawn; by day one stands at the top hedge, leaning on his spade
hook: A Southcote plough-book lies on the top terrace wall, the last line in a hand that is not a living one.

name: Briarfoot Watch
unique_feature: a tall square Warden tower with its stairs climbing round the outside, facing the shut south gate of the Briar and the grey thorn beyond it
story: The Wardens built Briarfoot to watch the Briar's south gate when it still opened, and kept it when it shut, because a gate nobody watches is a gate. Two Wardens keep it a season at a time and chalk what they see on the tally-board at the tower's foot: a thorn fallen, a light in the Briar, the grey a pace nearer the Southgate Stone.
encounter: two Wardens keep the tower; at midnight something from the grey comes up the terraces to the tower wall
hook: This season's tally-board has a line on it neither Warden will admit to chalking.

name: The Mother Pippin
unique_feature: a vast old apple tree lying half along the ground and rooted again where its limbs touched, ringed by the rows of the first orchard in the Vale
story: Every apple tree in Wickmere was grafted from this one, and every apple tree in Wickmere is in the Vale. Tamwick keeps it and wassails it on Candle Night, and its grafter cuts scions from it each winter for whoever will plant them. The tree fell in a gale before anyone's grandmother and did not die; it lay down and grew on.
encounter: the grafter by day; bristlebacks root the windfalls at dusk
hook: The grafter wants scions carried to a farm that has never had an apple tree, and none of them will take one.

name: The Scourers' Lodge
unique_feature: a long chalk-cob lodge under the Chalk Hound with its yard full of chalk carts, wooden rakes and rammers, and a white cord tied to the gate for every scouring the Hounders have made
story: The Hounders have scoured the Chalk Hound every seventh summer since it was cut: rake the turf off the figure, ram fresh chalk into it, and walk the whole outline singing, so the hound stays white and stays asleep. Seven years ago Aldous Hounder went down the swallet under Hound Down after a wolf that had come up out of it, and did not come back up. His widow has not called the scourers out this summer.
encounter: the Hounders live and work here
hook: Seventy-one white cords on the gate, one for each scouring, and no seventy-second.

name: The Listener's Shieling
unique_feature: a turf-roofed hut on the highest point of the Brow, its door facing the Hush, with a writing table out on the grass and a lantern hung on a crook beside it
story: On still nights the Brow sings: a few bars at a time, from nowhere, under the wind, in voices nobody has put a name to. The Wardens keep a Listener up here to write the verses down, because the Roll says Larkstead was known for its singing, and in a different hand, that they stopped. The Listener does not think they have stopped.
encounter: the Listener by day and half the night; the unquiet come up the cliff path when the singing is loud
hook: Three verses are missing from this year's book, one for each place the singing is loudest.

name: The Wheel Graves
unique_feature: a row of fresh graves on the open down east of Scathe, each marked with a cart wheel set upright in the turf
story: The Vale marks a carter's grave with his wheel. These are the carters who would not pay the Scathe tithe, and they were buried out here, in sight of the fort, by the carters who did pay and were ashamed. Bel Axtree tends them. Her man is the third wheel from the end.
encounter: the widow by day; at night the fort's lads come out to take the carters' boots
hook: Bel wants their names back out of the captain's book. The book says what was done to each of them, and she has not decided whether she wants to know.

name: The Roadmen's Lodge
unique_feature: the roofless lodge of the road crew that built the Vale's first roads, a pay-table still standing in its yard and a toll-bar across nothing
story: The crew that laid the Vale's roads lived here, and were paid off here the year the Toll fell, and the Wardens struck them from the Roll the winter after, because a crew with no road is nobody's neighbour. Their grandsons are the Larkbourne Boys. Once a year they come back to the lodge, stand in the yard and say their own names aloud to the pay-table, because nobody else will.
encounter: an old roadman lives in the one room with a roof; the Boys come by night to their table
hook: The crew's pay-book is under the pay-table, every name in it, and not one struck through.

name: The Wardens' Kennels
unique_feature: a ring of flint wall on Wardens' Down where the Rest keeps its hounds, the kennel yard empty and the gate chained from outside
story: The Wardens run hounds to follow the lost across the downs, nine couple of them, bred from a line older than the Rest. Three nights ago the whole pack went over the kennel wall at midnight without a sound and did not come back. The kennel-master chained the gate behind them so they would know it was shut to them, and has sat by it since.
encounter: the kennel-master and his girl by day; down wolves call at the wall after dark
hook: The hounds went west, toward Wolf Holt, and the kennel-master says they went the way a hound goes when it has been called.

name: The Struck Gibbet
unique_feature: three gibbets on the old drove over Bram Down with nobody hanging from them, only name-boards, painted and struck through, creaking in the wind
story: The Vale does not hang people. It hangs names. When the Wardens strike somebody from the Roll, their name is painted on a board and hung here on the drove where every flock goes by, and struck through, and left until the weather has it. The crows sit on the beams and the Larkbourne Boys come up at night to read who has joined them.
encounter: crows on the beams; two of the Larkbourne Boys come to read the boards after dark
hook: One board is new, and the name on it has not been struck through yet.

name: The Deneholes
unique_feature: a cluster of narrow shafts sunk into the top of Hound Down, each opening into a bell-shaped chamber in the chalk, one still with its windlass and a lid of hurdles
story: In the Ash Winter the Vale dug grain-pits on the high down where the ash could not settle, and lived through the year on what it had lowered into the chalk. Most have fallen in. One is still filled every Long Table with a sack from every farm on the down, for the next winter, and the lid is not lifted until the next winter comes.
encounter: bristlebacks root in the fallen pits; the kept pit is locked with a Warden's knot
hook: Somebody has lifted the lid of the kept pit and put it back crooked.

name: The Rookdown Bee-Garth
unique_feature: a round drystone garth on the down above Rookdown, its wall pierced with niches and a straw skep in every niche, and a bench by the gate for telling the bees
story: Rookdown tells its bees everything: a birth, a death, a wedding, a stranger in the village, the grey on the green. Bees that are not told leave. Old Tibby Wax keeps the garth and will tell them what you tell her, though she says it is better if you tell them yourself, from the bench, quietly, because they know when news has been carried.
hook: The bees have not been told about the grey on the green, and Tibby will not be the one to tell them.
